ECE 6612

Password verifiers and guesswork

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a password becoming a stored verifier and a later candidate being checked against that record.

A login server needs a repeatable way to check a submitted secret. At enrollment it chooses a fresh salt s and work settings c, then computes v = F(p, s, c), where p is the password and F is a suitable password-hashing function. The account record stores s, c and verifier v. On login it computes F(p′, s, c) for the submitted password p′ and compares the result with v. A successful check can establish a session; authorization then governs the resources that session may use.

A salt is public per-record data. Fresh independent salts make equal passwords produce different verifiers with overwhelming probability and force candidate calculations to depend on the particular record. An attacker who copies the database also gets those salts. Their security role is to separate work among records and defeat reusable precomputed password tables for the unsalted function.

Password-hashing functions such as bcrypt or scrypt deliberately make each guess costly; memory-hard designs add memory demands. Work settings choose the cost on the specified implementation and hardware. Fast general-purpose hashes make large guessing campaigns inexpensive. The user’s password distribution also matters: common words, reuse and predictable alterations give an attacker a productive guess order. Length and unpredictability increase the useful candidate space.

In an online attack, each guess reaches the service, where rate limits and additional factors can constrain it. In an offline attack, copied verifiers let the attacker test candidates on its own hardware. Service-side login limits therefore act on a different path from a database-leak guessing campaign. Protecting the record, increasing each guess’s cost and improving password choices address the inputs to that campaign.

Let D be the number of candidate passwords, N the number of independently salted accounts, t seconds per complete candidate/account calculation, and W identical independent workers. Testing every candidate against every record requires ND calculations. Ideal elapsed time is T = NDt/W seconds. This assumes fixed per-calculation cost and ideal scheduling; actual parallelism may be limited by memory, hardware and overhead. Finding a particular password earlier in the list changes the stopping time. Fig. 2 supplies a companion case: the mean search for one account whose secret is uniformly selected from 2^h candidates, where h is bits of uncertainty. About 2^(h−1) distinct guesses are needed on average. Its per-worker cost is entered in microseconds (1 µs = 10⁻⁶ seconds); increasing parallel workers increases the modeled aggregate guess rate.

After authentication, the session identifier becomes valuable evidence. It should be unpredictable, protected in transport, constrained by suitable cookie attributes, expired as appropriate and invalidated on logout or compromise. Multifactor authentication combines evidence categories; a password plus a second password still belongs to the knowledge category. Recovery and enrollment paths need comparable care because they can grant the same account access.

Example

For 60 independently salted accounts, 40,000 candidates, 0.012 seconds per complete calculation and 8 ideal workers, the full campaign costs 2,400,000 calculations. T = 60 × 40,000 × 0.012 / 8 = 3,600 seconds, or one hour. This is a work estimate for the stated candidate list and hardware, rather than a claim about a particular real password.

Sources and scope
  • C17 Web Authentication: verifier storage, salts, costly hashing, online and offline guesses.
  • RFC 7914: scrypt password-based key derivation.
  • NIST SP 800-63B: authentication factors, password-verifier and lifecycle considerations.

Practice

1. A stolen database contains 25 distinct salts and verifiers. An attacker tests 12,000 candidates against every account at 0.02 seconds per computation on five ideal workers. Find computation count and elapsed time.

Count candidate/account pairs, then multiply by seconds and divide by workers.

ND = 25 × 12,000 = 300,000 complete computations. Ideal time is 300,000 × 0.02 / 5 = 1,200 seconds, or 20 minutes. The model assumes the entire list is tested for every account and that five workers sustain the stated per-worker cost.

2. Two accounts chose the same password. Their records use fresh independent salts. Explain how this changes precomputation and what a database thief still needs to do.

Name the inputs to F for each record.

Each salt changes the candidate calculation, so one precomputed unsalted result cannot be reused as the verifier for both records. The thief has each public salt and settings, and can still compute F(candidate, salt, settings) and compare with that account’s verifier. Guess cost and password predictability determine the remaining effort.
